To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tumour invasion of the arterial system is facilitated by the presence of AV shunts and by the ligation of arteries.
tumours grow and metastasize by invading the arterial wall.

the arterial wall is resistant to neoplastic infiltration, that this resistance is lost when the normal structure of arteries and the normal dynamics and pressures of the arterial circulation are modified, and that the arterial wall can be modified in such a way that it becomes susceptible to neoplastic penetration and destruction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a new model of neoplastic invasion of arterial tissue.
the study of tumour-host interaction in the arterial wall and, in particular, the modification of tumour-host interactions by the surgical manipulation of the arterial circulation.
the development of a model of arterial tumour invasion and the modification of this process by surgery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the arterial circulation, as a system, is not only a barrier to the growth and spread of tumours but also a factor which modifies and influences tumour growth and spread.
the resistance of the intact arterial wall to tumour invasion is due to the normal structure of that wall and to its normal function in the circulation.

the arterial system is relatively resistant to invasion by tumour, that this resistance is dependent on the normal structure of arterial walls and on the normal dynamics of arterial circulation, and that the resistance is lost if arterial perfusion is reduced and/or the normal architecture of the arterial wall becomes modified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tumour cells can invade the arterial wall but that the process is slow and that the arterial wall is not a suitable site for metastatic implantation.
the resistance of systemic arteries is due to their normal structure and dynamics.

the normal arterial wall and the dynamics of the arterial flow are protective against tumour invasion and that this protection is lost if the arterial circulation is altered by ligation or by the formation of an AV anastomosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tumour invasion of arteries is a dynamic process and that the arterial circulation plays a significant role in the outcome.
tumour growth is influenced by the host's response to the presence of tumour, and this response can be altered by surgical intervention.
tumour invasion of the arterial system may not be an inevitable event.
